sub_answers.sub_question: Under what conditions of task orthogonality or high subspace overlap does overparameterization cease to reduce catastrophic forgetting?
How do label distribution shifts, nonstationary input covariances, or adversarial task sequences undermine overparameterization benefits?
What are theoretical failure modes when optimization deviates from NTK-like dynamics in finite-width or non-linear settings?
What empirical counterexamples demonstrate that mere parameter count increase does not guarantee continual learning robustness?
How does task similarity or covariance structure between sequential tasks impact the benefits of overparameterization?
sub_answers.text: Overparameterization’s benefit depends on task similarity: high feature learning (which can arise with less lazy, more feature-learning regimes) is only beneficial when tasks are highly similar [d110208s0p0]. Increasing model width helps only when it reduces feature learning and yields a lazier regime with lower forgetting, otherwise scale can hurt continual learning performance as the model transitions to richer feature learning [d110208s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What training protocols (e.g., learning rate schedules, batch sizes, single-pass vs multi-pass) interact with overparameterization effects?
sub_answers.text: Learning-rate schedules interact with forgetting: constant, intra-task decaying, and continuously decaying schedules affect how perturbations propagate across tasks, and restarting decay at task boundaries changes propagation of historical perturbations [d132661s0p0]. Batch-size and dynamic mini-batching change the one-pass variance and terminal-memory of stochastic error, so dynamic batch schedules influence the final risk via influence-weighted summaries of updates [d124268s0p0]. Single-pass (online) versus multi-pass regimes matter: single-pass Shuffle SGD has explicit bounds on final forgetting under convex objectives, showing per-task update counts and data amounts enter forgetting bounds differently than in multi-pass settings [d131842s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: How does memory or rehearsal (e.g., replay buffers) complement or substitute for overparameterization in linear continual settings?
What are the observed scalability limits of overparameterization benefits with increasing number of tasks in empirical studies?
What is the definition of linear continual learning in the context of sequential task training?
What is catastrophic forgetting and how is it quantified in linear models trained sequentially?
What empirical observations link model width or parameter count to forgetting in linear networks?
What theoretical frameworks (e.g., NTK, linear regression analyses) describe overparameterization effects in linear models?
sub_answers.text: One theoretical framework that directly analyzes overparameterization effects in continual learning is linear regression trained by stochastic gradient descent, studied for both underparameterized and overparameterized regimes [d96673s0p0]. Another related theoretical perspective characterizes the geometry of parameter space after task training (plausible regions resembling expanding cones and principal directions that affect forgetting) which informs constraints and regularizers to mitigate forgetting [d63301s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: How does the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) regime characterize training dynamics of overparameterized linear and linearized models?
sub_answers.text: In the NTK regime training dynamics of overparameterized or linearized models are characterized by a fixed, data-dependent kernel that governs learning as if training a linear model in function space [d120775s0p0]. This kernel perspective links dynamics to spectral properties of the input Gram/NTK matrix, so convergence and influence scale with the Gram/NTK spectrum and condition number [d120775s0p0][d131842s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: How does increased parameter dimensionality affect solution multiplicity and projection onto task subspaces in linear regression?
What role do orthogonality and subspace overlap of task feature vectors play in interference mitigation?
sub_answers.text: Constraining task updates to be orthogonal to directions important for prior tasks reduces interference by preventing new updates from altering critical prior-task components [d107377s0p0]. Learning task-specific low-rank subspaces that are kept orthogonal minimizes cross-task interference because tasks occupy disjoint parameter subspaces and thus do not project onto each other [d89976s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: How does implicit bias of gradient descent in overparameterized linear models influence retention of earlier task solutions?

For what quantitative levels of task feature orthogonality (e.g., cosine similarity of task subspaces, principal angles, or subspace overlap measured by projection matrices) does increasing model width stop decreasing forgetting—are there thresholds of subspace overlap or task rank beyond which additional parameters no longer mitigate interference?

In what specific ways do changes in class priors or label proportions, time-varying input second-moment structure (covariance eigenvalue shifts), or intentionally sequenced conflicting tasks (e.g., tasks with oppositely aligned gradient directions) negate the continual-learning advantages of overparameterized networks?

What formal failure modes can be proved or characterized when training departs from NTK/lazy-regime assumptions—for example in finite-width networks, feature-learning regimes, or when SGD noise and nonlinearity induce implicit bias—such that overparameterization no longer yields provable forgetting bounds?
sub_answers.text: Exiting the NTK/lazy regime into a feature-learning (rich) regime produces a transition to significantly more forgetting, i.e., overparameterization no longer guarantees low forgetting when feature learning is high [d110208s0p0]. [d110208s0p0] shows that increasing model width only helps when it reduces feature learning (laziness), so when training departs from lazy assumptions feature learning can induce substantial catastrophic forgetting. Formal analyses of online convex objectives show that forgetting bounds depend on task similarity and that these factors differ across objective classes, implying that NTK-style guarantees do not extend unchanged to feature-learning or finite-width settings [d131842s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Which empirical studies or reproducible experiments (e.g., on permuted/rotated MNIST variants, task-incremental CIFAR-100 splits, incremental Imagenet subsets, continual RL benchmarks, or transformer/ResNet architectures) show cases where simply scaling parameter count fails to prevent catastrophic forgetting, and what controlled ablations isolate why parameter growth does not help?
sub_answers.text: Experiments on Split-CIFAR-100 and Permuted-MNIST (PMNIST) demonstrate that the theoretical trends about forgetting beyond convex/NTK settings also appear empirically, indicating cases where scaling alone does not eliminate catastrophic forgetting [d131842s0p0]. [d110208s0p0] reports empirical studies and a reconciliation of prior contradictory scale results, showing that increasing width fails to reduce forgetting when it increases feature learning rather than laziness.

sub_answers.sub_question: In linear continual learning, how do different inter-task relationships—such as task similarity measured by cosine overlap, shared subspace dimensionality, or covariance matrix alignment—modify the gains from model overparameterization?

Which specific training regimen choices (for example: stepwise vs cyclic learning-rate schedules, large vs small batch sizes, single-epoch streaming versus multiple-epoch replay) have been shown to amplify or diminish overparameterization advantages in sequential-task experiments?
sub_answers.text: Different per-task learning-rate schedules (constant, intra-task decaying, and continuously decaying) change how perturbations propagate across tasks and thus affect forgetting and the benefits of overparameterization [d132661s0p0]. Restarting or resetting learning-rate decay at task boundaries alters propagation of historical sample perturbations and therefore modifies how overparameterization helps retain prior-task performance [d132661s0p0]. The number of updates per task and total number of task updates enter forgetting bounds and so amplify or diminish scale-related benefits (more updates per task change cumulative gradient alignment and its interaction with model scale) [d132661s0p0]. Increasing model width helps only when it reduces feature learning (i.e., yields a lazier regime); thus parameterization choices that increase laziness amplify overparameterization gains, while regimes that encourage rich feature learning can diminish them unless tasks are very similar [d110208s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: To what extent can explicit memory mechanisms (episodic replay buffers, reservoir sampling, rehearsal with sparsity constraints) replicate or enhance the benefits afforded by overparameterized linear models, and under which dataset regimes do they act as substitutes versus complements?

Empirically, how do reported performance improvements due to overparameterization degrade or saturate as the count of sequential tasks grows (e.g., performance vs task number curves, critical task counts, scaling exponents) in published linear or near-linear continual-learning studies?

Provide a precise operational definition of 'linear continual learning' when training linear models on a sequence of tasks: specify the training protocol (online vs. task-wise batches), objective functions, and what counts as preserved vs. updated parameters or features.

Define catastrophic forgetting in the context of linear predictors trained sequentially and list concrete, computable metrics used in the literature (e.g., accuracy drop per task, average forgetting, increase in task-specific loss, parameter projection overlap, or Fisher-based importance) with formulas or how they are measured across task boundaries.

Summarize empirical results that connect network width or total parameter count to forgetting in linear networks: cite experiments on two-layer and deep linear models that vary hidden dimension, overparameterization ratio, or sample-per-parameter regimes, and report the observed scaling laws, plots (forgetting vs width), and any counterexamples.

List and contrast the theoretical approaches used to analyze overparameterization effects for linear models: include Neural Tangent Kernel/linearization limits, exact linear regression and least-squares solutions, ridge regression and implicit regularization, random matrix theory analyses of eigenvalue spectra, and ODE/gradient-flow dynamics for finite- and infinite-width regimes.
sub_answers.text:
Analyses in the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) or linearization regime treat wide networks as effectively linearized around initialization and study forgetting through that linearized dynamics [d131842s0p0].

ev- and least-squares analyses for exact linear regression characterize forgetting by closed-form solutions and SGD behavior in under- and overparameterized linear models [d96673s0p0]. Convex-SGD analyses derive explicit upper bounds on expected final forgetting for strongly convex and general convex objectives, making forgetting depend on per-task sample sizes, task similarity, and task order [d131842s0p0]. Feature-learning perspectives analyze how signal and cumulative noise interact across tasks (e.g., in multi-view models) and use that to explain when replay recovers or fails to recover prior tasks [d119088s0p0]. Trajectory-geometry approaches study optimizer trajectories and principal directions (e.g., 'plausible cones' and top principal directions) to identify directions that cause forgetting and motivate constrained optimization that preserves intersections of task-specific parameter cones [d63301s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: In the NTK (Neural Tangent Kernel) limit and related linearized models, how do kernel eigenvalues, the fixed kernel approximation, and the Gram matrix spectrum determine the time evolution of training errors and parameter updates during gradient descent for overparameterized networks?

For linear regression with parameter dimension far exceeding input dimension, how does increasing the number of parameters change the size of the solution set (nullspace dimension), the structure of minimum-norm versus other interpolating solutions, and the projected components of solutions onto task-relevant feature subspaces (e.g., row space vs nullspace)?

Quantitatively, how do the angle, cosine similarity, or overlap between different tasks' feature vectors or subspaces (mutual coherence, principal angles) predict the degree of interference or cross-talk between tasks, and how do orthogonalization or low-overlap representations reduce interference in linear multi-task settings?

Which specific implicit biases does (full-batch) gradient descent induce in overparameterized linear models (e.g., convergence to minimum-norm / pseudoinverse solutions, alignment with top singular vectors), how do initialization scale and learning rate affect that bias, and how do these factors determine retention or forgetting of earlier-task solution components?

In which precise regimes of task similarity — e.g., fully orthogonal task subspaces, high principal subspace alignment, or shared versus disjoint feature supports — does increasing model width or parameter count stop yielding reductions in catastrophic forgetting? Specify quantitative measures (subspace angles, canonical correlations, rank overlap) and thresholds where overparameterization ceases to help.

By what mechanisms do nonstationary label priors (class imbalance drift), changing input covariance structure (feature distribution shifts or context-dependent covariances), or an adversarially ordered sequence of tasks (interleaved opposing labels, label permutation attacks) negate the continual-learning advantages of large neural networks? Cite how each type of distribution shift breaks the assumptions behind overparameterization benefits.

What rigorous theoretical breakdowns occur when training dynamics depart from the NTK/linearized regime — for example due to finite width effects, strong feature learning, non-smooth activations, or adaptive optimizers — and which formal results (loss landscape changes, absence of kernel limit, unstable tangent kernel) predict failures of overparameterization to prevent forgetting?

Which empirical studies or controlled experiments show concrete cases where simply increasing parameter count (wider or deeper nets, overcomplete representations) fails to improve or even worsens retention across sequential tasks — include dataset/task pairs, model families, training protocols, and measured metrics (forgetting gap, backward transfer) that demonstrate this negative result?

In sequential learning of linear or kernel models, how does the similarity structure or covariance between consecutive tasks (e.g., task alignment, overlap in input covariance matrices, principal subspace overlap) quantitatively affect the gains from increasing model width or parameter count?

Which specific training regimes (fixed vs decayed learning rates, batch size scaling, single-pass online SGD vs multi-epoch training, momentum, adaptive optimizers like Adam) change how overparameterization influences generalization and forgetting in continual or sequential-task settings?
sub_answers.text: An appropriate choice of step size (learning rate) helps mitigate forgetting in both underparameterized and overparameterized settings [d96673s0p0]. Different learning-rate schedules—constant, intra-task decaying, and continuously decaying—change how sample perturbations propagate and thus alter forgetting, with restarting decay at task boundaries affecting propagation across tasks [d132661s0p0]. Single-pass (online) Shuffle SGD has distinct forgetting behavior and admits explicit upper bounds on expected final forgetting, showing that single-pass online training regimes qualitatively affect how overparameterization influences forgetting [d131842s0p0]. Increasing model width is beneficial only when it reduces the amount of feature learning (i.e., moves the training toward a 'lazy' regime), so the degree of feature learning controlled by parameterization interacts with how overparameterization affects generalization and forgetting [d110208s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: In linear continual learning setups, how do explicit memory/rehearsal mechanisms (replay buffers, reservoir sampling, stored exemplars, generative replay) interact with model overparameterization—do they reduce the need for larger models, provide complementary benefits, or serve as a substitute under formal/empirical measures of forgetting and transfer?

Across empirical continual-learning experiments, where overparameterization was varied, what are the observed limits to its benefits as the number of sequential tasks grows (e.g., task counts where benefits saturate or reverse, scaling laws, breakdown points reported in studies using benchmarks like permuted MNIST, split CIFAR, or synthetic linear tasks)?
How is 'linear continual learning' formally defined when training a sequence of tasks on linear models, including task distribution, update rules, and evaluation protocol?

How is catastrophic forgetting characterized for linear predictors trained sequentially, what metrics (e.g., average forgetting, backward transfer) are used, and how are they computed for linear least-squares or ridge models?

What empirical studies or experiments report relationships between network width/parameter count and forgetting in linear or linearized networks, including specific dataset/task setups and measured forgetting trends?

Which theoretical analyses — for example kernel/NTK limits, closed-form linear regression solutions, or dynamics of GD on overparameterized linear models — explain how overparameterization influences learning and forgetting in linear continual-learning settings?
sub_answers.text: Analyses in the kernel / NTK regime have been used to study continual learning and overparameterization effects on forgetting [d131842s0p0]. Closed-form and dynamical analyses of linear regression (including SGD dynamics in under- and overparameterized regimes) provide theoretical insights into how overparameterization affects forgetting in linear predictors [d96673s0p0]. Convex-SGD analyses deriving explicit upper bounds on expected final forgetting (for strongly convex and general convex objectives) connect per-task data, task similarity, and ordering to forgetting, and these analyses include overparameterized settings among the regimes considered [d131842s0p0]. Feature-learning analyses of replay methods identify signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and signal accumulation as key factors that determine whether replay (and thus overparameterized feature learning) prevents or allows forgetting [d119088s0p0]. Frameworks that formalize an ideal continual learner and derive generalization bounds (e.g., ICL) link rehearsal and other mechanisms to provable prevention of forgetting and thus relate to overparameterized solution concepts in continual learning [d84965s0p0].

As the number of parameters grows beyond the number of data points in linear regression, how does the increasing nullspace dimension change the count and structure of solutions, and how does it quantitatively alter the projection (e.g., projected norm or cosine) of learned parameter vectors onto specified task subspaces or feature directions?

Quantitatively, how do pairwise inner products, principal angles, or subspace overlap between different tasks' feature vectors control cross-task interference and the degree to which learning one task perturbs components relevant to another (including thresholds where interference becomes negligible)?

Which implicit biases of gradient-based optimization in overparameterized linear models (such as convergence to minimum-norm interpolants, dependence on initialization, effect of step size or early stopping, and the role of stochastic noise) determine how much of an earlier task's solution is preserved when subsequently training on new tasks?
